newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU struggles to agree budget rules for euro.
newsitem.headline: EU struggles to agree budget rules for euro.

text.p: European finance ministers worked into the night on Thursday in a bid to pin down the details of an elusive agreement on budget discipline under a single European currency.
The talks have been stalled by Germany's demands for ultra-tough sanctions on countries running excessive budget deficits once they have signed up to economic and monetary union (EMU).
It was not clear whether the ministers would be able to agree on Thursday or whether they would have to hand over the problem to a summit of EU leaders starting in Dublin on Friday.
Diplomats said Germany remained isolated in its demands, but Swedish finance minister Erik Asbrink said there had been "movement" on the German side and he was hopeful of a deal.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who dreamt up the idea of a stability pact to ensure budget discipline in EMU, had talked tough ahead of the meeting, telling the Bonn parliament, "I will not move away from the clear stability goal."
But Asbrink said, "The German finance minister has shown openess and moved." He said everyone around the table wanted a deal before the meeting concluded. "So I'm optimistic."

Failure to clinch an accord over the next few days would upset financial markets where there is concern that disagreement over the details of a single currency might throw the whole concept into doubt.

At issue at the Dublin talks is Germany's insistence that countries in a single currency bloc should be fined for running budget deficits of more than three percent of national output and that there should be only clearly defined exceptions.

The German government, eager to gain popular support for the single currency project, is determined to ensure that the economic framework for the euro is strict enough to produce a single European currency which is a robust as the German mark.
Bonn's partners want greater flexibility and are asking Germany to make it easier for offending nations to avoid sanctions if their economies are in trouble.
Germany's current proposals envisage nations being exempt from fines if their economies contract over 12 successive months. The size of the contraction is what the ministers were knocking heads over.
The stability pact is a key element of a report on economic and monetary union (EMU) due to be studied by EU leaders at the summit proper, which begins on Friday.

Other aspects of the report have already been informally agreed. They include the legal basis for the euro and a new post-EMU exchange rate mechanism to keep EU currencies outside the euro bloc stable.
The EU leaders were also due to discuss at the summit the bloc's long-term future, in the shape of a draft EU treaty written by the Irish EU presidency.
"What we are aspiring towards is bringing Europe closer together. We want to see a closer union of the peoples of Europe," Irish Prime Minister and summit host John Bruton said.

The Irish draft treaty shows the majority of countries are heading towards closer cooperation in crime fighting, joint employment policies, stronger foreign policy links and a true border-free Europe with common asylum and immigration policies.
It also calls on the EU to create an area of freedom, security and justice ensuring the free movement of people.

Of all the leaders coming to Dublin, British Prime Minister John Major will be among the most watched. With his ruling Conservative party torn apart over Europe, Major will be under pressure not to appear too conciliatory to his EU colleagues.
Britain opposes most of the proposals under discussion for the draft treaty -- which is supposed to prepare the bloc for enlargement into central and eastern Europe.
London also has an opt-out on the single currency, making discussions on post-EMU life something of a political minefield for the embattled British leader.
